idiom_name: constructor-returned closures capturing state; small interfaces composed by struct embedding
implementation_notes: Go has no component host in the standard library, so the reusable unit becomes a language-level idiom: a constructor function returns closures or a small struct that captures its state (function literals are first-class per the language specification), and composition happens by calling one constructor from another or by embedding a small interface. State shared across goroutines gets a mutex, channel or sync primitive, and that fact becomes part of the unit's contract; effects are goroutines with explicit cancellation through context.Context and defer for cleanup, replacing a UI runtime's lifecycle hooks. Inside WASM UI kits the same constructors are wrapped in component lifecycles, but the reusable unit stays a storage-owning value; prefer a plain struct with methods once there are more than a handful of operations, since that is Go's normal composition form rather than a wrapper.
pitfalls: Closures capture variables by reference: a loop variable captured by several closures sees its final value unless it is re-declared per iteration (the pre-Go-1.22 semantics), silently aliasing several units to one state.
State captured in closures is invisible to the type system and cannot be copied safely; expose a struct with methods when callers need references, equality or serialization.
Goroutines started by the unit keep running after the caller loses interest unless a context or stop channel is part of the returned contract.
